title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem 848 asks for the maximum size of A ⊆ {1,...,N} such that ab + 1 is never squarefree for all a, b ∈ A. Solved by Sawhney: the answer is ⌊N/25⌋ for large N.
mathContext: The problem sits at the intersection of extremal combinatorics and multiplicative number theory. The non-squarefreeness constraint $ab + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ for some prime $p$ forces elements of $A$ into specific residue classes. The extremal sets are arithmetic progressions mod 25, arising from $5^2 \mid ab + 1$ when $a \equiv b \equiv 7$ or $18 \pmod{25}$.

title: Mathlib Imports
content: Imports Mathlib.Tactic, Mathlib.Data.Nat.Basic, and Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Basic. The Tactic import provides general proof automation; Nat.Basic provides arithmetic; Prime.Basic provides the Nat.Prime predicate used in the squarefree definition.
mathContext: The imports are minimal: no Finset.LocallyFiniteOrder or ZMod is needed because the file axiomatizes all results rather than proving them computationally. A richer formalization might use $\mathbb{Z}/25\mathbb{Z}$ from `ZMod` to prove the mod 25 construction.

title: IsSquarefree Definition
content: Defines `IsSquarefree n` as: for all primes p, p² does not divide n. Equivalently, in the prime factorization n = Π p^{aₚ}, all exponents aₚ are 0 or 1. This is the constructive (predicate) form rather than Mathlib's `Squarefree` which uses the algebraic definition via `IsUnit`.
mathContext: The density of squarefree numbers among $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.608$ (Euler product over $1 - 1/p^2$). Since most numbers are squarefree, requiring $ab + 1$ to always be non-squarefree is a genuinely restrictive constraint. The definition $\forall p,\, p.\text{Prime} \to \neg(p \cdot p \mid n)$ is equivalent to Mathlib's `Squarefree` but more computationally transparent.

title: Non-Squarefree Product Property
content: Defines `HasNonSqfreeProductProp A`: for ALL pairs a, b ∈ A (including a = b), the product ab + 1 is not squarefree. The axiomatized `maxNonSqfreeSet N` gives the maximum cardinality of such a set in {1,...,N}, with the trivial bound maxNonSqfreeSet(N) ≤ N.
mathContext: The condition includes the diagonal $a = b$, so $a^2 + 1$ must be non-squarefree for every $a \in A$. Since $a^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ has exactly 2 solutions mod $p^2$ when $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ (and 0 solutions when $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$), the self-pair constraint already forces $A$ into a union of residue classes modulo squares of primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. The axiom `maxNonSqfreeSet_le` records the trivial upper bound.

title: Mod 25 Construction
content: Axiomatizes `mod25_achieves`: for a ≡ b ≡ 7 (mod 25), we have 5² | ab + 1. This is because 7·7 + 1 = 50 = 2·5², and more generally a·b + 1 ≡ 49 + 1 = 50 ≡ 0 (mod 25) for any a, b in this residue class.
mathContext: The computation: $7 \cdot 7 + 1 = 50 = 2 \cdot 25$, so $25 \mid 7 \cdot 7 + 1$. For general $a = 25s + 7$ and $b = 25t + 7$: $ab + 1 = (25s+7)(25t+7) + 1 = 625st + 175s + 175t + 50 \equiv 50 \equiv 0 \pmod{25}$. The residue $18$ works identically: $18 \cdot 18 + 1 = 325 = 13 \cdot 25$. Note $7 + 18 = 25$ and $7 \cdot 18 = 126 \equiv 1 \pmod{25}$, reflecting that $\pm 7$ are the square roots of $-1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/25\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Lower Bound: N/25
content: Axiomatizes `lower_bound`: for N ≥ 25, maxNonSqfreeSet(N) ≥ ⌊N/25⌋. This follows immediately from mod25_achieves: the set {n ∈ {1,...,N} : n ≡ 7 (mod 25)} has size ⌊N/25⌋ and satisfies HasNonSqfreeProductProp.
mathContext: The lower bound $\lfloor N/25 \rfloor$ gives density $1/25 = 0.04$. The hypothesis $25 \leq N$ ensures the set is non-empty. This is a simple counting argument: in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, there are exactly $\lfloor N/25 \rfloor$ elements $\equiv 7 \pmod{25}$ (namely $7, 32, 57, \ldots$).

title: Van Doorn's Upper Bound
content: Axiomatizes van Doorn's density bound: maxNonSqfreeSet(N) · 1000 ≤ 108 · N + C for some constant C. This encodes the real-valued bound |A|/N ≤ 0.108... using integer arithmetic to avoid real numbers in Lean.
mathContext: The density bound comes from: $|A|/N \leq 2 \sum_{p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}} 1/p^2$. The factor 2 arises because $x^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ has 2 solutions for $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. The sum converges: $1/5^2 + 1/13^2 + 1/17^2 + 1/29^2 + \cdots \approx 0.054$, giving $2 \times 0.054 \approx 0.108$. The integer encoding $\text{max} \cdot 1000 \leq 108 \cdot N + C$ avoids real-number formalization entirely.

title: Sawhney's Exact Solution
content: Axiomatizes `sawhney_solution`: there exists N₀ such that for all N ≥ N₀, maxNonSqfreeSet(N) = ⌊N/25⌋. This closes the gap between the N/25 lower bound and van Doorn's 0.108N upper bound, confirming the mod 25 construction is globally optimal.
mathContext: Sawhney's theorem: $\text{maxNonSqfreeSet}(N) = \lfloor N/25 \rfloor$ for $N \geq N_0$. This is remarkable because the gap between $1/25 = 0.04$ and $0.108$ seemed large—one might have expected a denser construction using multiple primes. The result says the single prime $p = 5$ (the smallest $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$) completely determines the extremal density. The existential quantification $\exists N_0$ means the result is non-effective: the threshold is not computed.

title: Structural Characterization of Extremal Sets
content: Axiomatizes `sawhney_structure`: any extremal set of size N/25 for large N must consist entirely of elements ≡ 7 (mod 25) or entirely of elements ≡ 18 (mod 25). No mixing is possible—the two extremal families are disjoint.
mathContext: This rigidity result is stronger than the size determination. It says: if $A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $|A| = \lfloor N/25 \rfloor$ and $ab + 1$ is never squarefree, then $(\forall a \in A,\, a \equiv 7 \pmod{25})$ or $(\forall a \in A,\, a \equiv 18 \pmod{25})$. The impossibility of mixing follows from: if $a \equiv 7$ and $b \equiv 18 \pmod{25}$, then $ab + 1 \equiv 7 \cdot 18 + 1 = 127 \equiv 2 \pmod{25}$, so $25 \nmid ab + 1$ and the shared factor mechanism breaks.

title: Why 25? The Role of p = 5
content: The modulus 25 = 5² arises because 5 is the smallest prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4). The equation x² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p²) has solutions only when p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and the smallest such prime gives the densest residue class (density 1/p²). The primes 13, 17, 29,... give sparser classes (1/169, 1/289, ...), so p = 5 dominates.
mathContext: For $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, $-1$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$, so $x^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ has 2 solutions. By Hensel's lemma, these lift to 2 solutions mod $p^2$. The density of each residue class is $1/p^2$. For $p = 5$: density $1/25 = 0.04$. For $p = 13$: density $1/169 \approx 0.006$. Since we need the entire set in one residue class, $p = 5$ gives the largest set. Sawhney's deep result shows no clever combination of multiple primes can beat the single-prime construction.
